\title{Source-Bound Validation and Contract-Indexed Accounting for Constant-Shape LLM Workflows}
\author[vit]{Nambi Rajan M}\ead{nambirajan.m2024@vitstudent.ac.in}

\begin{abstract}
Hiding prompt contents does not hide a workflow's model identities, token counts
or instrumented tool events. OrchLang is a bounded language whose compiler aligns
secret paths, pads model usage and completes loops with cover events. An
executable Lean validator establishes conditional usage-trace noninterference.
Source-bound acceptance prevents a proposed repair from choosing its own original
program or secrecy policy. A compositional certificate establishes trajectory
admission from explicit value, tokenizer, response and tool contracts.
We implement a byte-bounded adapter and check concrete candidates for twelve
workflow variants. The Python frontend and native serving code remain trusted.
Independent interpreters agree on 6,320 finite audit executions. A full study of
\roundTwoPairs{} real-model pairs on one frozen implementation preserves all
saved fields and gives one shaped logical trace per workflow. Main-study median
weighted logical overhead is \roundTwoMedian{} times original usage.
A separate single-batch native-prefill prototype fixes the batch-size projection,
but sequence metadata still reveals request length and one batching configuration
fails visible-output preservation. The contribution is an executable integration
of source-bound validation, contract-indexed accounting and admission for bounded
LLM workflows. Timing protection, provider billing equivalence and physical
failure noninterference require additional serving contracts.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

An LLM application can hide every prompt from its dashboard and still reveal
which path it took. A support workflow may classify a private message, call a
specialist on one route, and repeat generation on another. Ordered model identities
and token counts can reveal the route without revealing the message. Token-count
and routing-metadata attacks already establish this
threat~\cite{weiss2024prompt,zhang2024timewilltell,chen2026routing}. The programming problem is
how to control the usage of an entire bounded workflow while preserving the
results on which later decisions depend.

Constant-resource programming, control-flow balancing, padding and translation
validation are established techniques~\cite{agat2000transforming,ngo2017constant,
wang2014supersequence,pnueli1998tv}. Applying them to LLM workflows introduces an
execution-contract problem. An operation includes a request, tokenizer, chat
template, decoding caps and visible-response rule. Two operations with equal
caps need not select equal response kernels, and token counts in one model's unit
do not bound another model's requests. A validator's guarantee also depends on
the original program and secrecy declarations against which it checks the repair.

OrchLang makes these boundaries explicit. Its untrusted shaper proposes padding,
dummy calls and bounded-loop completion. A trusted reader independently derives
the original core and declared secrets from source; Lean checks erasure, labels,
randomness sites and caps. Execution counts each complete request before
dispatch, checks returned usage and retains generated token IDs and request
hashes. A per-model reservation ledger refuses unsupported budgets and retains
reservations when dispatch usage cannot be confirmed.

The system studied here consists of the Python frontend and runtime and the Lean
core validator. Source-bound checking connects these components: the compiler
may propose a repair, but it cannot choose the original or the secrecy policy
against which that repair is checked. Earlier certificate experiments are retained
as historical supplementary material rather than components of this architecture.

We position OrchLang as an offline programming and assurance tool for a declared
logical reporting contract. A workflow author can inspect a proposed repair,
validate it against the actual source and inspect its model-indexed envelope
before deciding whether a particular serving interface supports that contract.
Deployment confidentiality additionally requires an independently enforced observer
and a supported admission domain.

The paper makes three contributions. First, source-bound acceptance connects
declared secrets and useful requests to an executable translation validator.
Second, model-indexed accounting and a compositional admission certificate connect
fixed shapes to resource envelopes under explicit primitive contracts. Third,
independent operational comparisons and real-model records test the implementation
and expose its limits. These contributions adapt established resource and
translation-validation methods to bounded LLM workflows.

\section{Observation and scope}\label{sec:scope}

The observer receives an ordered list of events
\[
e ::= \mathsf{llm}(m,t_{\mathrm{in}},t_{\mathrm{out}})\mid\mathsf{tool}(f).
\]
Here $m$ denotes a model contract and $f$ a tool name. Contents, site IDs, dummy
flags, natural stopping lengths and private audit records are excluded. Tool
events are logical instrumentation: a dummy tool event does not invoke a real
external service. An external tool provider or packet observer therefore requires
a different execution contract.

The prototype's event is an accounting record produced by a trusted wrapper.
In isolated-padding mode, that wrapper aggregates a filler prefill and an
unchanged request prefill into one input count. An observer below the wrapper
can distinguish those submissions and recover the actual request length. The
implementation therefore evaluates fixed resource envelopes and budget
reservations; it does not enforce input-length confidentiality at the model server.
For an observer restricted to exported logs, permitted report normalization gives
the same trace abstraction without dummy inference. Our normalization baseline
is consequently a practical alternative, not an inadmissible defense.

Executing cover work remains useful for testing whether an envelope can actually
be consumed and reconciled against local records. That engineering purpose does
not itself provide a security advantage over normalization. A serving interface
that enforces a fixed external trace would require a separately specified adapter,
including its batch metadata, cache behavior, stopping policy and failures.

The model and trusted host may see secret contents. The theorem concerns a
separate usage observer and excludes elapsed time, streaming, packets, shared
caches, failures, concurrency and contents. A retained latency-augmented attack
illustrates this boundary: it reaches 100 percent balanced accuracy in one workflow.
Constant logical usage does not imply constant running time.

For stores $\sigma\equiv_{\lo}\tau$ agreeing on public variables, usage
noninterference requires equal traces under each fixed randomness tape. Public
inputs may select different traces. A globally constant shape is a stronger case
used by the evaluated secret-input workflows.

The \emph{source contract} binds exact bytes, original core, slots and declared
secrets. The \emph{model contract} binds artifact hash, template/tokenizer family,
stop policy, optional decoding grammar and padding mode. The \emph{execution contract} defines admission,
logical accounting, forced output and visible prefix. Scalar source token
annotations help size targets; they are not sound bounds transferred between
tokenizers. Before dispatch, the host counts the fully rendered request in the
receiving model's unit and refuses overflow instead of silently shortening it.
A refusal may itself reveal information. Protection including failures requires
a supported admission domain and compatible failure protocol. Section~\ref{sec:domain}
proves both a restricted-domain result and a compositional sufficient admission
condition. Section~\ref{sec:concrete-admission} implements guarded byte bounds for
the pinned local adapters. Native correspondence and a physical failure refinement
remain separate obligations.

\section{Language and shaping}

\subsection{Bounded programs}

The source language has labelled text inputs, model profiles, templated prompts,
capped calls, pure tools, conditionals and bounded loops. For example:
\par\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
\begin{lstlisting}
workflow Router {
  input q: text secret max_tokens 48;
  model m = "llama1b";
  prompt classify(x) = user "Classify: {x}";
  prompt respond(x) = user "Answer: {x}";
  let route = call classify(q) using m max_tokens 3;
  if route == "short" {
    let answer = call respond(q) using m max_tokens 16;
  } else {
    let answer = call respond(q) using m max_tokens 64;
  }
  output answer;
}
\end{lstlisting}
\end{minipage}\par
Unshaped usage exposes request lengths and the selected cap. Shaping fixes the
classification usage and aligns the response arms while retaining their visible
caps. The core contains sequencing, calls, tools, dummies, conditionals and loops.
Expressions contain literals, variables, concatenation, tool-argument escaping
and template-level message trimming.
Argument escaping prevents separator characters or backslashes from changing argument
boundaries and is represented in Lean as well as Python.

Labels form $\lo\sqsubseteq\hi$. Flow-insensitive propagation joins argument and
program-counter labels. A high call requires fixed usage, a high conditional
requires equal arm shapes, and a high loop requires a shaped body completed to
its public bound. Model responses inherit the confidentiality of their requests.
Figure~\ref{fig:grammar} gives the complete core grammar and its relation to the
surface syntax. The rules below use the same constructors as the executable
Lean definitions.

\subsection{Targets, padding and output}

The compiler sizes targets from tokenized literals, variable caps and slack.
This is an execution-envelope heuristic. Subword concatenation and cross-model
values invalidate a general scalar-bound claim. An audit example used a string
counted as one BERT token whose complete GPT-2 request required 259 tokens against
an 18-token target. Exact complete-request admission addresses that boundary.
The earlier exact-tokenization study is summarized in the historical supplement;
neither observation proves arbitrary static tokenizer bounds.

Default isolated padding prefills filler in a separate context, resets it and
evaluates the unchanged request. Logical input usage sums filler and request
counts. This is an accounting stress test: two submissions remain distinguishable
below the wrapper, and neither single-call input hiding nor equal compute time
follows from their sum.
In-band filler changes the visible prompt and may change responses. Legacy
truncation remains explicitly selectable for reproduction but is not the default
publication configuration.

Forced decoding generates $N$ token IDs, continuing past a stop token when needed.
The workflow receives the prefix before the first stop, cut to its original cap
$k\leq N$. The logical output unit is the returned ID list: natural calls exclude the
terminating stop ID, while forced calls count all $N$ IDs, including stop and
post-stop IDs. Re-encoding decoded text is not an equivalent count, and provider
EOS-accounting conventions may differ. Under fixed serving behavior, isolated padding and prefix
extraction are intended to preserve the natural response; this remains an explicit
assumption and an empirical check. The implementation recognizes EOS and declared
single-token stop IDs. It rejects empty or multi-token stop declarations before
workflow execution, because string-level matching across a visible-cap boundary
is outside its semantics.

\subsection{Alignment and loops}

A two-sequence dynamic program aligns compatible model contracts or equal tool
names, merges counts by componentwise maximum and inserts missing dummy events.
For the evaluation weight $t_{\mathrm{in}}+4t_{\mathrm{out}}$, it minimizes the common
two-arm profile cost. Each contract receives input weight one and output weight four for this scalar
score. This is a chosen decode-sensitive objective, not a tokenizer conversion or
measured price. Section~\ref{sec:costs} varies the output weight while
holding workflows and model contracts fixed.
Multi-arm alignment is progressive and heuristic; nested shaped constructs are
atomic. Global optimality is not claimed. These mechanisms adapt balancing and
supersequence defenses~\cite{agat2000transforming,wang2014supersequence}.

After early loop termination, ghost iterations emit the body's shape without
updating the store or reading real-site randomness. Model dummies perform real
local generation. Dummy tool events only add instrumented records, avoiding
external effects. The loop emits its shape repeated to its declared bound.
Figure~\ref{fig:semantics} makes the store and randomness behavior explicit.

\section{Validation and mechanized properties}\label{sec:formal}

\subsection{Acceptance from a bound source}

Translation validation checks each proposed transformation rather than trusting
the optimizer~\cite{pnueli1998tv,necula2000tv}. The source reader derives the
original, declared secrets, slots and labels independently of candidate code.
A candidate cannot replace the original or omit secrets by supplying a weaker
list. The JSON interface requires an explicit list and checks that every listed
input is high. Because a hash identifies bytes without proving their interpretation,
the Python parser, lowerer and serializer remain trusted.

A small end-to-end negative case makes the source binding consequential.
For a source-declared secret query, a candidate supplies an empty secret list and
an unshaped natural call. The core checker accepts that call under the weakened
all-public policy. The source-bound entry point re-derives the secret declaration
and rejects the same call; it accepts the compiler's padded repair. The executable
\code{experiments/source\_binding\_case.py} retains all three actual Lean verdicts.
This is a policy-omission attack on an unbound interface, not an unsoundness in the
core validator under its supplied policy.

Lean checks the padding discipline, separated high/public randomness sites,
visible caps no larger than forced lengths, and equality of normalized erasures.
Erasure removes padding, dummies and loop-completion flags. Useful requests cannot
be changed, reordered or dropped. Only SHA-pinned aliases with identical template,
stop, decoding-grammar and padding contracts share a model identity. Experiments verify weight bytes.
Figure~\ref{fig:validation} states the label and acceptance rules. The source-bound
rule separates the trusted reader's responsibility from the checked core premises.

\subsection{World and hypotheses}

Execution is parameterized by a world $w$ containing tokenization, natural and
forced generation, padding, visible-prefix extraction and pure tools. A tape
$\omega(i,j)$ supplies randomness to the $j$th execution of site $i$. Dummies and
ghost iterations do not advance real-site counters. Pointwise equality induces
equal trace laws for a common secret-independent tape distribution. Lean includes
the direct finite weighted-list form, not a measure-theoretic library or a verified
physical random generator.

Two explicit propositions state the primitive assumptions:
\begin{align*}
\mathsf{Conforms}(w):\quad&
\operatorname{tok}_m(\operatorname{padReq}_m(T,r))=T,\\
&\operatorname{outTok}_m(\operatorname{forced}_m(r,c,N))=N;\\
\mathsf{Transparent}(w):\quad&
\operatorname{view}_m(k,\operatorname{forced}_m(
\operatorname{padReq}_m(T,r),c,N))\\
&\hspace{12mm}=\operatorname{gen}_m(r,k,c)\qquad(k\leq N).
\end{align*}
These quantify over the abstract world's arguments. The runtime is partial and
rejects unsupported requests; a total refinement into this world is not proved.
A post-dispatch count check detects a violation but cannot retract exported usage.

\subsection{Conformance on an admitted domain}\label{sec:domain}

Global conformance is stronger than a nontruncating padder can offer: an arbitrary
target may be smaller than the request. The separate development
\code{proof/AdmissionDomain.lean} replaces that premise with
$\mathsf{ConformsOn}(w,D)$. Here $D(m,T,N,r)$ identifies supported request contracts;
the two conformance equations are required only for members of $D$, for every
randomness cell. For example, a concrete domain must exclude oversized requests
and unsupported context/output limits.

The recursively defined $\mathsf{RunsIn}(w,\omega,D,p,s)$ checks membership for
every padded call actually reached, including model dummies and loop-completion
calls. It follows evaluated intermediate stores and loop guards. It does not
assume that scalar source input caps imply membership. The observation alphabet
adds refused, completed(trace), failed(prefix) and unknown-dispatch(prefix).
An ideal admission adapter emits completed core execution exactly when RunsIn
holds, and refused otherwise. This is a noncomputable specification, not a
physical preflight algorithm that predicts future responses without inference.

\begin{theorem}[Restricted-domain shape and admission]
If $\operatorname{shape}(p)=s$ and $w$ conforms on $D$, each execution satisfying
RunsIn emits exactly $s$. Two initially empty-trace executions have equal ideal
completion/refusal observations if their RunsIn predicates are equivalent.
A domain certificate establishing RunsIn for every advertised input and every
tape makes every such observation completed($s$).
\end{theorem}

The declarations \code{shape\_exec\_on}, \code{admitted\_noninterference} and
\code{certified\_domain\_noninterference} prove these statements by structural and
loop induction. They require neither global conformance nor transparency.
The domain certificate is an explicit proof obligation. RunsIn itself is a
trajectory predicate, so evaluating it is not a preflight algorithm for a chain
whose later prompts depend on generated text. In the physical runtime, a first
call can complete before a later rendered request exceeds its target. One run
then exposes failed($[e_1]$), while another completes with $[e_1,e_2]$.
Per-call refusal prevents overspending at the next dispatch but does not hide
this prefix-length channel. The sufficient certificate below addresses request
admission; transport failures and unknown dispatches remain outside its claim.

An executable falsification uses two public-equal stores: a short secret completes,
while an oversized secret is refused before dispatch. Thus resource-safe rejection
alone does not prove failure-observation noninterference. A separate exhaustive
check covers the 15 strings over $\{a,b\}$ of length at most three, under three
seeds in the character-token mock world: all 45 executions complete with the
static shape. This finite check illustrates premise checking; it does not certify
arbitrary strings, model trajectories or stochastic tapes.

\subsection{Compositional static admission}\label{sec:static-admission}

An admission certificate can avoid lookahead by bounding the values from which
every request is constructed. Let $|r|_b$ measure text size in a declared unit,
such as UTF-8 bytes, and let the finite vector $v$ bound every store slot.
The invariant is $I_v(\sigma)\equiv\forall x,|\sigma(x)|_b\leq v_x$,
with unlisted slots bounded by zero. Define the computable expression envelope
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_v(s)&=|s|_b,& E_v(x)&=v_x,\\
E_v(e_1{+\!+}e_2)&=E_v(e_1)+E_v(e_2),&
E_v(\mathsf{escape}(e))&=2E_v(e),\\
E_v(\mathsf{trim}(e))&=E_v(e).
\end{aligned}
\]
The envelope contract requires subadditive concatenation, at most twofold
escaping and nonexpansive trimming. It also supplies receiving-model token bounds
$\mathsf{tok}_m(r)\leq\alpha_m|r|_b+\delta_m$, visible-response bounds
$|\mathsf{view}_m(k,\mathsf{forced}_m(\mathsf{padReq}_m(T,r),a,N))|_b
\leq\rho_m(k)$ for $k\leq N$, and tool-result bounds $\theta_f$.
These are primitive assumptions with a common text-size unit, not conversions
between two models' token counts. A concrete implementation must justify them.

For each padded call, the checker tests
\[
\alpha_m E_v(e)+\delta_m\leq T,\qquad
T+N\leq C_m,\qquad k\leq N,\qquad\rho_m(k)\leq v_x.
\]
Tool assignments require $\theta_f\leq v_x$. Dummies are checked against their
actual fixed request and context limit. Both conditional arms and sequence
components must pass. Loops require a certified body and, when padded, a certified
cover profile. No call to \code{exec} or RunsIn occurs in this checker.
An input guard checks $I_v$ before the first dispatch; the proof preserves this
invariant through every useful assignment and leaves it unchanged under cover work.

\begin{theorem}[Static certificate implies trajectory admission]
Let the envelope contract hold for $w$, and let the compositional checker accept
$p$ under $v$. For every initial store satisfying $I_v$ and every tape $\omega$,
$\mathsf{RunsIn}(w,\omega,D_b,p,s)$ holds, where
$D_b(m,T,N,r)\equiv\mathsf{tok}_m(r)\leq T\land T+N\leq C_m$.
The final store also satisfies $I_v$.
\end{theorem}

Store preservation is proved by \code{static\_certificate\_sound}.
The theorem \code{static\_certificate\_implies\_RunsIn} establishes admission
by statement and loop induction. \code{static\_certificate\_domain} supplies
the premise of the restricted-domain theorem for all inputs satisfying the guard.
With conformance on $D_b$ and a fixed shape, every admitted core execution therefore
completes with that shape. This result removes the trajectory-lookahead obligation
for certified envelopes; it does not assume a prediction of future model text.

The optional byte-bounded frontend implements this sufficient checker on
source-derived candidates. It guards input buffers, bounds tool results and
applies a declared UTF-8 response buffer after decoding. Targets use $E_v$ rather
than a heuristic conversion between token units. The exported candidate and
finite bounds are checked by Lean's actual \code{staticCertificate}, and the
source-bound validator separately checks erasure and secrecy. Section~\ref{sec:concrete-admission}
reports all twelve application candidates and their execution checks.
The ordinary frontend retains its heuristic mode. The bounded mode is a separate
execution contract applied to both original and shaped programs; it is not a
claim that every unbounded original fits the chosen buffers. Native tokenization,
decoder correspondence and physical failure behavior remain trusted obligations.

\begin{theorem}[Core usage noninterference]
Under Conformance, a program accepted by the padding and randomness-site checks
has equal usage traces from public-equal stores for every tape.
\end{theorem}
The proof inducts over statements. Public calls use equal requests and tape cells;
high calls emit fixed usage; high branches emit a common shape; public branches
select the same arm. Loop induction handles real and ghost iterations. Confinement
preserves public stores and public-site counters under a high program counter.

\begin{theorem}[Core functional preservation]
Under Transparency and the cap check, a padded program and its normalized erasure
end in the same store for every initial store and tape. An accepted candidate
therefore preserves the corresponding unpadded original's store.
\end{theorem}
The declarations \code{validateProgram\_sound} and \code{secret\_inputs\_sound}
combine these checks with declared-secret labelling. Neither property implies
task accuracy or verifies the source reader.

\subsection{Model-indexed budgets}

Let $U_m(s)$ be the triple of input-token sum, generated-token sum and call count
in trace $s$ for contract $m$. Tool events contribute zero to this triple.
Different model units remain separate coordinates.
\begin{theorem}[Shape accounting and budget admission]
If $\operatorname{shape}(p)=s$ and $w$ conforms, then every store and tape give
$U_m(\operatorname{trace}(\operatorname{exec}(p)))=U_m(s)$. If
$U_m(s)\leq B_m$ componentwise, execution stays within $B_m$.
\end{theorem}
The declarations \code{shape\_usage\_exact} and \code{shape\_budget\_sound} are
direct corollaries of \code{shape\_exec}, not a new cost logic. The runtime admits
a complete shape against budgets before inspecting inputs. Without a complete
shape, only per-call reservations apply. The Python ledger is tested, not a
mechanized refinement or concurrent ownership system.

Accounting alone cannot replace the ordered shape check. For distinct fixed
events $A$ and $B$, paths $[A,B]$ and $[B,A]$ have the same per-contract totals
but different observations. A common profile such as $[A,B,A]$ preserves each
path's useful order by filling its missing position with a dummy. Conversely,
equal caps cannot justify replacing a request with different text: the response
kernel may change even when usage does not. The erasure check and model contract
therefore complement the budget theorem rather than following from it.

Lean 4.19.0 checks the development without admissions. Noninterference and validator
axiom reports contain only \code{propext} and \code{Quot.sound}; the budget
corollaries require only \code{propext}. JSON decoding correctness, parsing,
concrete tokenizers and backend code remain outside the formal boundary.
The domain extension's shape proof also uses only \code{propext}; the ideal
admission results additionally use Lean's classical choice and quotient axioms.
Neither development uses a \code{sorryAx} placeholder.

\section{Implementation and custody}

The runtime admits complete requests, reserves usage before dispatch and confirms
counts/caps on return. Transport exceptions or nonconforming returns leave usage
incomplete, with reservations retained rather than recorded as zero-cost success.
Private request/token evidence supports inspection without entering classifier features.
Each manifest binds source, dataset, selected IDs, implementation hashes, model
contracts, decoding parameters, platform, threads and optional backend-library
hashes. Resume requires the same manifest and rejects duplicate or foreign IDs.
Unbound historical records cannot be silently resumed under the new runtime.

A separate \code{python -m orchlang check} command re-reads source and model
bytes to check an exported artifact. It does not trust the artifact's original
or secret declarations. Request hashes and token-ID records allow separate
checks of the declared model contract and the wrapper's aggregate counts.
These records complement the proof: they can expose a concrete disagreement
without establishing correctness for every tokenizer input or physical execution.

\section{Related work}

The program-counter security model formalizes control-flow
observations~\cite{molnar2005pc}. Verified constant-time compilation preserves
an appropriate observation model through compiler
passes~\cite{barthe2020ctcompcert,barthe2021constantresource}. OrchLang instead
checks a proposed core translation. Its source reader and physical serving
adapter remain trusted, and its observation consists of workflow accounting events.

Agat, constant-resource typing/synthesis and FaCT establish language-based
mitigation~\cite{agat2000transforming,ngo2017constant,cauligi2019fact}. RelCost and
probabilistic relational logics are more general reasoning
frameworks~\cite{cicek2017relcost,avanzini2025erhl}. OrchLang specializes established
ideas to bounded model operations; its budget result is a fixed-shape corollary.
Supersequence defenses and Pacer establish padding and deployment
precedents~\cite{wang2014supersequence,mehta2022pacer}. Our observation excludes
their network/timing setting. Token-count and routing attacks already motivate
the threat~\cite{weiss2024prompt,zhang2024timewilltell,chen2026routing}.

Predictive mitigation makes a different tradeoff: delayed releases can bound
timing leakage while changing performance~\cite{askarov2010predictive,zhang2012timing}.
That approach is relevant when a fixed admission envelope cannot be guaranteed.
It would require an explicit model of releases, overflows and repeated
observations; a time bucket alone does not establish the logical noninterference
proved here.

LMQL combines model calls, control flow and output
constraints~\cite{beurer2023lmql}. Its decoding constraints address the language of
responses, whereas OrchLang constrains an execution's usage observation. A
categorical-output constraint changes the response kernel. Our separate CRAG
ablation evaluates that change under its own grammar-indexed contract.

SICC compiles policy-relative communication; communication-graph work studies
workflow metadata and cover traffic~\cite{xu2026sicc,dangol2026graph}.
Exact logical input/output counts are a scope distinction, not evidence that
earlier work ignores workflow structure. CaMeL, FIDES and Hard-KLAIM address
agent integrity, information flow, provenance or
authority~\cite{debenedetti2025camel,costa2025fides,aldinucci2026hardklaim}.
Hard-KLAIM's adapter assumptions are particularly relevant. Proof-Carrying
Contracts likewise distinguishes formal commitments from world
correspondence~\cite{ciliberto2026pc2}. Authorization and usage noninterference
are different properties.

Resource admission overlaps Token Budgets and structural workflow-bound
tools~\cite{khan2026budgets,dickerson2026loom,costwright2026,typedresources2026}.
Our sequential ledger is not affine ownership or verified concurrency. Two narrow
retained Costwright probes are not a general benchmark. The supplement provides
a source-by-source matrix. The literature search does not establish exclusive priority.

\section{Limitations and implications}

The checker and conditional core theorems are mechanized. Source parsing,
serialization, native tokenization and physical serving are trusted. Finite
cross-layer agreement tests that boundary without closing the proof gap. The
byte-bounded adapter defines an explicit advertised input domain; refusal outside
that guard can reveal information. Successful context checks do not establish
device-memory availability, transport success or a physical failure protocol.
Side effects, concurrency and stateful tools require richer semantics before
entering the theorem's observer.

The application corpus is authored and small. Bounded ports change upstream
models, retrieval and loop choices, and poor task outputs remain poor after
shaping. A retained census codes 37/54 example applications as content-dependent
from 72 listed rows; it is not a population estimate or an independently
double-coded study. Single-machine classifiers and paired runs cannot establish
deployment security or general usefulness.

The practical artifact lets an author validate a source-bound repair, inspect
its per-model envelope and select either heuristic admission or a declared
byte-bounded interface. The static certificate removes trajectory lookahead under
explicit primitive contracts. It does not verify those native contracts or turn
the sequential Python ledger into a concurrent ownership system.

The native-prefill prototype enforces one fixed batch-size projection, but full
sequence metadata reveals the real-token subset. Its microbatch-dependent
output mismatch also shows why attention isolation alone is insufficient to
assume transparency. A deployment needs an observer-specific serving refinement,
including metadata, caches, stopping and failures. Paced execution and public loop
envelopes would require separate leakage and deadline-miss measurements.

\section{Conclusion}

OrchLang connects source-declared secrecy to checked workflow shapes,
model-indexed accounting and compositional admission. The optional byte-bounded
adapter makes the admission certificate executable on actual workflow candidates.
A homogeneous study of \roundTwoPairs{} real-model pairs preserves saved outputs
and fixed logical traces, while independent records expose the conventions behind
those counts. The native-prefill experiment fixes a narrower batch-size observer
and retains both metadata leakage and a transparency counterexample. These
results support an offline programming and assurance artifact whose physical
serving guarantees depend on separately justified adapters.

\section*{Data and software availability}
The accompanying versioned artifact contains source, execution records, protocols,
generated tables, dependency versions and SHA-256 integrity manifests. Model
weights are obtained separately using the supplied revision and hash pins.
The historical repository is
\url{https://github.com/guyoverclocked/orchlang-compiler-design-project}; the
revised sources and evidence are supplied in the accompanying review archive.
Reproduction instructions identify the implementation associated with each cohort.

\section{Evaluation}\label{sec:evaluation}

The evaluation separates four questions: whether the implementations agree on
the checked core, whether one frozen implementation preserves application
outputs, whether source-derived byte envelopes pass the admission certificate,
and which native observations survive a single-batch serving prototype.
All inference is local. The full application study and the three additional
experiments below have separate protocols and denominators.

\subsection{Core checks and implementation identity}

All 47 configured tests pass, including source binding, immutable resumption,
model-indexed reservations, unsupported stop declarations, complete token-piece
decoding and pre-dispatch byte guards. Actual pinned GGUFs enable the tokenizer
and template tests; model-free runs report those cases as skips.
Generated differential testing retains 1,000 authored programs, 5,000
original/candidate Lean checks and 16,000 trace/store comparisons without a
counterexample. A separate operational comparison covers 150 programs in four
contexts under two finite kernels and five variants, plus a targeted template
program: Python, an independent interpreter and Lean's actual \code{exec} agree
on 6,320 executions and 604 validator checks. These audit worlds use character
counts. They test implementation agreement without verifying the frontend or
native tokenizer. Retained fault injection rejects all 103 mutants that leak
under its finite oracle, among 210 mutants over 12 operators.

Before application inference, we froze production code at \code{41a7d81} and ran
from a clean detached checkout. All nine main workflows and three Qwen variants
use that identity. Manifests bind the complete implementation, source, data,
selected IDs, model contracts and native-library hashes. The study uses Python
3.12.14, llama-cpp-python 0.3.36, native build 11490 (\code{9c2e0e491}), four CPU
threads, a 4,096-token context, batch size 128 and greedy decoding. GPU execution
uses Vulkan on an NVIDIA RTX 5050 Laptop GPU, with 99 requested offload layers.
Seeds are fixed by dataset index and useful-call site. We report logical usage;
this single-machine protocol supports no throughput or timing-protection claim.

\subsection{Full homogeneous application study}\label{sec:final-validation}

The main study contains 1,172 paired inputs over routing, chaining,
evaluator--optimizer, orchestrator--worker, switch, email, calculator, corrective
RAG and adaptive RAG. It uses Llama 3.2 1B, with Llama 3.2 3B for the adaptive
workflow's larger-model path. Replication contains 512 Qwen 2.5 1.5B pairs over
switch, email and corrective RAG. The bounded ports retain their declared loop
limits, retrieval corpora and primary grading prompts. Failed or mismatched
attempts cannot be removed from the completion denominator.

All \roundTwoPairs{} pairs complete with equal saved fields, one shaped trace
per workflow and no recorded truncation. The independent record audit checks
3,368 execution records and \roundTwoCalls{} useful and cover model calls.
It re-tokenizes every complete request, reconstructs visible prefixes, reconciles
per-model ledgers and matches private local eval/yield records to public events,
including duplicate multiplicities. A deliberately changed input count is
detected. These records support the declared client accounting contract; they
are not provider attestations or a proof of every intermediate store value.

respectively, using the inherited scorers. Calculator remains a control-flow

\subsection{Cost and observer alternatives}\label{sec:costs}

For input weight one and output weight four, main-study median overhead is
\roundTwoMedian{} times original usage, with range
\roundTwoMin{}--\roundTwoMax{}. These weights describe logical usage, not a
provider invoice. Static recompilation on these records gives zero median
saving against all-branches cover execution, with 52 percent maximum saving;
uniform model cells give 16 percent median and 59 percent maximum saving.
These are comparisons of validated envelopes, not new executions of commercial
defenses. The supplement retains actual alignment/all-branches/uniform/random
executions of the separate two-route microbenchmark.
Recompilation at output weights 0.25, 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 accepts all 72 candidates
and leaves each of the twelve variants' shapes unchanged. This tests the given
profiles rather than establishing weight insensitivity for arbitrary programs.

For an observer restricted to exported reports, normalization achieves the same
fixed reporting abstraction with less execution work. Isolated prefill is useful
for consuming and auditing an envelope; it adds no input-length protection below
the wrapper. Historical latency-augmented attacks reach 100 percent balanced
accuracy on one shaped workflow. The present study therefore makes no timing
claim. All earlier application cohorts retain their original implementation
identities in the supplement and do not enlarge this homogeneous denominator.

\subsection{Concrete byte-bounded admission}\label{sec:concrete-admission}

The optional adapter in Section~\ref{sec:static-admission} is instantiated for
all twelve workflow variants. We scan every vocabulary entry of each pinned
GGUF with the complete native token-piece API: the two Llama vocabularies each
contain 128,256 entries and Qwen contains 151,936. All three have maximum raw
piece length 128 bytes. There are 231 pieces longer than 32 bytes in each Llama
vocabulary and 240 in Qwen. The former fixed-buffer wrapper returned an empty
piece for a 128-byte witness; the corrected decoder resizes the buffer and
retains the complete piece. No generic 32-byte bound is assumed.

The adapter explicitly bounds UTF-8 input buffers, visible responses and tool
results. A response buffer has size $128k$ for visible token cap $k$; it is
applied after decoding, because replacement decoding of invalid UTF-8 can expand
the byte count. Tool and input buffers use four times their declared token
annotation, as a chosen byte policy rather than a tokenizer conversion theorem.
Both original and shaped executions use the same buffers. The frontend derives
slot bounds from all source assignments and sizes each target with $E_v$.
It then exports the actual candidate and bounds to Lean's
\code{staticCertificate}, alongside independent source-bound validation.

For these byte-BPE tokenizers we declare $\alpha_m=1$ and $\delta_m=0$ on valid
UTF-8 complete requests, with automatic BOS insertion disabled. Every vocabulary
contains all 256 single-byte pieces. The native byte-splitting/merge algorithm
remains trusted~\cite{llamacpp2026vocab}; 2,058 adversarial and seeded complete
requests per model have no counterexample to the bound. Arbitrary isolated
non-UTF-8 byte strings are outside the source-string domain. A Lean lemma proves
that bounded token-piece lengths and a token cap bound the sum of raw piece
bytes; the adapter's post-decoding buffer enforces the actual string bound.
The scan and executable certificate do not verify native code or JSON parsing.

\subsection{Single-batch native prefill}\label{sec:native-prefill}

We also implement a separate greedy prototype using one native
\code{llama\_decode} submission with 128 tokens. Useful request tokens occupy
sequence 0 and filler occupies sequence 1; each sequence has its own positions,
and only the last useful token requests logits. Subsequent decode submissions
contain one token. Sequence membership provides attention isolation through the
native batch interface~\cite{llamacpp2026batch}. This experiment runs on CPU with
two model families, three empty/short/multilingual prompt bodies, visible caps
4 and 16, and forced length 24. All attempts remain in Table~\ref{tab:round2-native}.

Microbatch size 1 preserves all 12 visible outputs. At size 128, one Qwen case

observations refute unqualified transparency for the latter configuration;
they do not prove transparency for every input at size 1.
Sequence and logit metadata still identify the useful-token subset in every
case. The prototype therefore supports a fixed native-size projection, while a
server observing full batch metadata retains request-length information.
No claim extends this projection to packets, cache traffic, elapsed time or
arbitrary physical failures.

\subsection{Categorical corrective-RAG ablation}

The primary Qwen grader mixes numeric-score instructions with a yes/no parser.
The earlier retained diagnosis found 484 zeros, 34 ones, five yes responses and
77 no responses among 600 grades; accepting numeric ones still sent all 150
questions to web search. We retain that primary port and evaluate a separate
contract: a categorical relevance prompt and a grammar permitting only
\code{\{"score":"yes"\}} or \code{\{"score":"no"\}}. The grammar is part
of the grader's model-contract identity. Answer generation, retrieval and the
rule ``search if any of four grades is not yes'' remain the same.

The ablation runs all 150 paired questions. All 600 original grades are valid
categorical JSON: \categoricalYes{} yes and \categoricalNo{} no. Web search is
selected for \categoricalSearch{} questions and omitted for
\categoricalNoSearch{}. Task accuracy is \categoricalTask{} percent under the
same inherited answer scorer: \categoricalCorrect{}/150 correct, compared with
\categoricalPrimaryCorrect{}/150 for the primary Qwen port. The paired comparison
has \categoricalImproved{} improved and \categoricalRegressed{} regressed answers.
The route distribution remains strongly imbalanced. All pairs preserve saved fields, including the
four grades, and have one shaped logical trace. Format compliance does not
establish grader correctness, and this combined prompt/grammar intervention
does not identify either component's individual causal contribution.
